source.title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics

accepted.question_text: Let G=(V,E,ω) be a weighted simple graph, let d_G be the geodesic distance on V induced by G, and let ε>0. A subset L⊂V is an ε-net if (i) every vertex v∈V lies within distance ε of some landmark u∈L and (ii) every two distinct landmarks u_i,u_j∈L satisfy d_G(u_i,u_j)>ε. Determine optimal upper and lower bounds for the number of elements of an ε-net for G.
accepted.context_brief: Dowker complexes and ε-nets on metric graphs

evidence.quote: Definition 1.5 (-net). Let (V, dG) be the finite metric space obtained from the weighted graph G = (V, E, ω). Given L = {u1, u2, . . . , ul} ⊂ V and  ≥ 0 then: (i) The set L is an -sample of G if ... for any v ∈ V there exists uj ∈ L such that dG(v, uj ) ≤ . (ii) L is -sparse if for any two distinct points ui, uj ∈ L, their distance dG(ui, uj ) > . (iii) The set L is an -net of G if it is an -sample of G and is -sparse.
Open Problem 1.1. Given a weighted simple graph G = (V, E, ω) and  > 0, determine optimal upper and lower bounds for the number of elements of an -net for G.

accepted.question_text: Let G=(V,E,ω) be a weighted simple graph. Construct an algorithm that computes an ε-net L⊂V for G and simultaneously improves on the existing ε-net algorithms by using fewer landmarks and running in less time than the currently available methods.

evidence.quote: Three different methods to obtain -nets in metric graphs, namely, the greedy, iterative and SPTpruning algorithms, are proposed in [1]. These algorithms are experimentally compared with respect to the number of landmarks they produce for the same graph, including their execution time.

Open Problem 1.2. For a weighted simple graph G = (V, E, ω), propose an algorithm to construct an -net for G such that: (i) It is based on a lower number of landmarks than that of the existing algorithms; (ii) The time of execution of the algorithm is lower than the existing algorithms.

accepted.question_text: Let G=(V,E,ω) be a weighted simple graph, let W=V be the witness set, and let L⊂V be an ε-net. The Dowker complex Dow_α(W,L) is the simplicial complex on the landmark set L whose simplices are the subsets σ⊂L for which there exists a witness w∈W satisfying d_G(w,l)≤α for every l∈σ. Determine how to choose ε and how to select the ε-net L so that, for sufficiently large α, the one-dimensional persistence diagram PD_1(Dow_α(W,L)) has cardinality equal to the genus of G. Assuming such an ε-net is given, find a bound for the bottleneck distance d_B(PD_1(VR_α(G)), PD_1(Dow_α(W,L))) in terms of the cycle lengths of G and ε.

evidence.quote: Definition 1.4 (Dowker Complex). Let G = (V, E, ω) be a weighted simple graph with induced geodesic distance dG, and let L, W ⊂ V. For α ∈ R≥0, let Dowα(W, L) be the abstract simplicial complex with set of vertices L and a simplex σ ∈ Dowα(W, L) if and only if there exists w ∈ W such that dG(w, l) ≤ α for all l ∈ σ.

Open Problem 1.3. Let G = (V, E, ω) be weighted simple graph. Take the set of witnesses W = V. (i) Determine  > 0 and the way to select an -net L ⊂ V such that PD1(Dowα(W, L)) has cardinality equal to the genus of G, for a sufficiently large value α. (ii) Assuming that an -net for G satisfying (i) is given. Find a bound for dB(PD1(VRα(G)), PD1(Dowα(W, L))), in terms of the lengths of cycles in G and , where dB is the bottleneck distance in persistence diagrams.

accepted.question_text: Let G=(V,E,ω) be a weighted graph with landmark set L⊂V and witness set W⊂V. For the Dowker complexes built from G, study stability in two directions. First, if G'=(V,E,ω') has the same vertices and edges as G but a different weight function ω', bound the bottleneck distance between the persistence diagrams of the Dowker complexes of G and G' in terms of the supremum distance between ω and ω'. Second, if L and L' are both ε-nets for G, find conditions under which Dow_α(W,L) and Dow_α(W,L') have the same homotopy type.

evidence.quote: Open Problem 1.4. Let G = (V, E, ω) be a weighted graph and let L, W ⊂ V be sets of landmarks and witnesses for G. (i) Let G' = (V, E, ω') be the metric graph with the same set of vertices and edges of G, but another weight function ω'. Find a bound for the bottleneck distance of the persistence diagrams corresponding to the Dowker complexes of G and G' in terms of the supremum distance between ω and ω'. (ii) If two sets of landmarks L and L' for G are -nets. Find conditions on the landmarks, such that Dowα(W, L) and Dowα(W, L') have the same homotopy type.

accepted.question_text: Fix positive integers n and t, an integer m with 1≤m≤2^n−1, and an n×m binary matrix A whose columns a_1,…,a_m are distinct nonzero vectors in {0,1}^n. For an n×t binary matrix x=(x_1^T,…,x_t^T), define the i-th expressiveness indicator by m_i^A(x)=Σ_{j=1}^t <a_i,x_j>_2, where the inner product is taken in GF(2) and the outer sum is taken over the integers. If x and y are sampled uniformly at random, the computational problem asks for P((m_i(x)=m_i(y)) for all i). For fixed m and k≤m, determine this probability when A consists of all binary vectors of weight at most k.

evidence.quote: Fix n, t ∈ Z+ and let 1 ≤ m ≤ 2^n − 1. ... A = (aT1, . . . , aTm) where ai ∈ {0, 1}^n for 1 ≤ i ≤ m. Moreover, the {ai}mi=1 are non-zero and pairwise distinct.

Definition 2.2 (Expressiveness Indicator). Given A, x as above and 1 ≤ i ≤ m, we define the ith expressiveness indicator mAi (·) as: mAi (x) := Σ^t_j=1 <ai, xj>2 where the inner product <·, ·>2 is mod 2 but the outer sum is integral.
Computational Problem. Given A, let x and y be sampled uniformly at random. Compute: P ((mi(x) = mi(y)) ∀i)
Open Problem 2.1. Fix m and k ≤ m. Can we answer Computational Problem when A consists of all vectors of weight at most k?

accepted.question_text: With the same setup as the computational problem for the expressiveness indicators m_i^A(x), classify the families of nonzero binary column sets A for which the probability P((m_i(x)=m_i(y)) for all i), with x and y sampled uniformly at random, can be computed exactly, and classify the families A for which that probability can be computed efficiently.
accepted.context_brief: Exact and efficient solvability by choice of A

evidence.quote: Computational Problem. Given A, let x and y be sampled uniformly at random. Compute: P ((mi(x) = mi(y)) ∀i)
Open Problem 2.2. For which choices of A can we answer Computational Problem exactly? For which choices of A can we answer Computational Problem efficiently?

accepted.question_text: In the same computational problem where A is an n×m binary matrix with distinct nonzero columns and one must compute P((m_i(x)=m_i(y)) for all i) for uniformly random n×t binary matrices x and y, determine whether this computational problem is NP-complete when A is arbitrary.

evidence.quote: Computational Problem. Given A, let x and y be sampled uniformly at random. Compute: P ((mi(x) = mi(y)) ∀i)
Open Problem 2.3. Is Computational Problem NP-Complete for arbitrary A?

accepted.question_text: In the same computational problem for the expressiveness indicators m_i^A, determine for which families of binary column sets A one can approximate the probability P((m_i(x)=m_i(y)) for all i) when x and y are sampled uniformly at random.

evidence.quote: Computational Problem. Given A, let x and y be sampled uniformly at random. Compute: P ((mi(x) = mi(y)) ∀i)
Open Problem 2.4. For which choices of A can we approximate answers to Computational Problem?

accepted.question_text: Let H=(V,E) be a 4-uniform hypergraph with source node s and sink node t. For a bipartition {S,̄S} with s∈S and t∈̄S, let ∂_i(S) be the set of hyperedges having exactly i vertices on the smaller side of the cut, and assign penalty w_i≥0 to each hyperedge in ∂_i(S), with w_0=0. The cardinality-based hypergraph s-t cut problem minimizes Σ_i w_i |∂_i(S)| subject to s∈S and t∈̄S. When w_1=1, determine the computational complexity of this problem in the regime w_2>2.
accepted.context_brief: 4-uniform hypergraph s-t cuts with convex split penalty

evidence.quote: Edges with i nodes on the small side of the cut are denoted by ∂i(S) = {e ∈ E : min{|e∩S|, |e∩S¯|} = i}. ... The cardinality-based hypergraph s-t cut problem is given by (1) min_S⊆V Σ_i wi |∂i(S)|, subject to s ∈ S and t ∈ S¯.
Open Problem 3.1. What is the complexity of the cardinality-based 4-uniform hypergraph s-t cut problem when w2 > 2 and w1 = 1?

accepted.question_text: Consider a 4-uniform hypergraph H=(V,E) with source node s and sink node t. In the No-Even-Split 4-uniform s-t cut problem, one must separate s and t while minimizing the number of 1-vs-3 hyperedge splits and forbidding any 2-vs-2 hyperedge splits. Determine the computational complexity of this problem.

evidence.quote: This limit converges to the No-Even-Split 4-uniform s-t cut problem: minimize the number of 1-vs-3 hyperedge splits when separating s and t, without making any 2-vs-2 hyperedge splits.
Open Problem 3.2. What is the complexity of the No-Even-Split 4-uniform s-t cut problem?

accepted.question_text: Let G=(V,E) be a directed acyclic graph. In front-elimination of an edge (i,j), one removes that edge and adds edges from i to every successor of j; in back-elimination, one removes (i,j) and adds edges from every predecessor of i to j. A complete edge elimination sequence is a sequence of such eliminations that transforms G into the corresponding bipartite DAG representation of the Jacobian, and its cost is the sum of the individual elimination costs. Given G and an integer k≥0, determine whether there exists a complete edge elimination sequence whose total cost is at most k.

evidence.quote: Definition 4.1 (Edge Elimination). Let G = (V, E) and (i, j) ∈ E. Front-elimination of (i, j) yields ... Back-elimination of (i, j) yields ... By the chain rule of differentiation, all complete edge elimination sequences transform G into a bipartite dag representing the Jacobian matrix of the underlying numerical program. The cost of an edge elimination sequence is the sum of the costs of the individual edge eliminations.
Open Problem 4.1 (Edge Elimination). Given a directed acyclic graph G and a positive integer k ≥ 0, is there a complete edge elimination sequence with cost less than or equal to k?

accepted.question_text: Let G=(V,E) be a directed acyclic graph. Eliminating a vertex j removes j and adds every edge (i,k) with i a predecessor of j and k a successor of j; the cost of eliminating j is |P_j|·|S_j|. A complete vertex elimination sequence is a sequence of such eliminations that transforms G into the corresponding bipartite DAG representation of the Jacobian, and its cost is the sum of the individual elimination costs. Given G and an integer k≥0, determine whether there exists a complete vertex elimination sequence whose total cost is at most k.

evidence.quote: Definition 4.2 (Vertex Elimination). Let G = (V, E) and j ∈ V. Elimination of j yields ... at the cost of |Pj| · |Sj|. ... all complete vertex elimination sequences transform G into a bipartite dag representing the Jacobian matrix of the underlying numerical program. The cost of a vertex elimination sequence is the sum of the costs of the individual vertex eliminations.
Open Problem 4.2 (Vertex Elimination). Given a directed acyclic graph G and a positive integer k ≥ 0, is there a complete vertex elimination sequence with cost less than or equal to k?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a directed acyclic graph arising from a numerical program, and suppose one wants to reverse G while using persistent memory of size at most M and computational cost at most O, where persistent memory stores values that cannot be recomputed for free and computational cost counts the work needed to recover overwritten intermediate values during reversal. Given integers M≥n and O≥0, determine whether G can be reversed within persistent memory at most M and computational cost at most O.
accepted.context_brief: DAG reversal under memory and cost constraints

evidence.quote: The combinatorial DAG Reversal problem aims to minimize the computational cost of data flow reversal in limited (≪ O(p^2)) persistent memory.

Open Problem 5.1 (DAG Reversal). Given a DAG G and two integers M ≥ n and O ≥ 0 can G be reversed within persistent memory of size less than or equal to M with computational cost less than or equal to O?

accepted.question_text: Let M be an n×n real matrix with spectral radius λ=ρ(M)<1, partitioned into an ℓ×ℓ array of blocks. For a delay matrix δ with zero diagonal, define the asynchronous update operator M^(δ) by allowing block i at the next step to depend on block j from δ_{ji} steps earlier. If every delay is bounded by k, is it always true that ρ(M^(δ))≤λ^(1/(k+1))? If not, does there nevertheless exist a function f:(0,1)×N→(0,1) such that ρ(M^(δ))≤f(λ,k)?

evidence.quote: To build a simple model of asynchronous updates for M, we partition the matrix M into an ℓ × ℓ array of blocks and for each i ∈ [ℓ] define the update scheme x˜(k+1)_i = Σ_j Mij x˜(k−δji)_j.

Open Problem 6.1. Let M be a n × n real matrix with p(M) = λ < 1 partitioned into an ℓ×ℓ array of blocks. Is it the case that for all elements δ of [k]ℓ×ℓ with zero diagonals, ρ(M(δ)) ≤ λ^(1/k+1)? If not, is there some function f : (0, 1) × N → (0, 1) such that ρ(M(δ)) ≤ f(λ, k)?

accepted.question_text: Let G=(V,E) be a graph and let k≥0. A set Z⊂V is an (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set if, for every set E' of at most k edges, Z remains a zero-forcing set for the graph (V,E\E'). For sparse graphs resembling power-grid networks, determine whether one can give a structural characterization of the minimum-size (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing sets, in particular for graphs with few cycles or for sparse graphs of large diameter.

evidence.quote: Definition 7.3 ((n − k)-contingent Zero Forcing). Given a graph G = (V, E), a set Z ⊆ V is a (n − k)-contingent zero-forcing set if for every set of edges E0 of size at most k, Z is a zero-forcing set for G0 = (V, E − E0).
Open Problem 7.1. Is there a structural characterization of the minimal-sized (n − k)-contingent zero-forcing sets for graphs with few cycles? For sparse graphs with large diameter?

accepted.question_text: Let G=(V,E) be a graph and let k≥0. A set Z⊂V is an (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set if it remains a zero-forcing set after deletion of any set of at most k edges. Determine whether there is an efficient algorithm for finding a minimum-size (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set for graphs with few cycles or, more generally, for sparse graphs with large diameter.

evidence.quote: Definition 7.3 ((n − k)-contingent Zero Forcing). Given a graph G = (V, E), a set Z ⊆ V is a (n − k)-contingent zero-forcing set if for every set of edges E0 of size at most k, Z is a zero-forcing set for G0 = (V, E − E0).
Open Problem 7.2. Is there an efficient algorithm to determine the minimal-sized (n − k)-contingent zero-forcing set for graphs with few cycles? For sparse graphs with large diameter?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with structural properties characteristic of power grids, and let k≥0. A set Z⊂V is an (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set if it remains zero-forcing after deletion of any set of at most k edges. Determine the typical size of a minimum (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set, expressed in terms of the numbers of vertices and edges, for graphs with power-grid-like structure.
accepted.context_brief: Typical contingent zero-forcing size in power-grid-like graphs

evidence.quote: Definition 7.3 ((n − k)-contingent Zero Forcing). Given a graph G = (V, E), a set Z ⊆ V is a (n − k)-contingent zero-forcing set if for every set of edges E0 of size at most k, Z is a zero-forcing set for G0 = (V, E − E0).

Open Problem 7.3. What is the typical size, in terms of the number of vertices and edges, of the minimal (n − k)-contingent zero-forcing sets in graphs exhibiting structural properties characteristic of power grids?
